export_note: Selected fields from the completed native grade; machine-local paths are omitted. The mathematical grade is preserved.

grade.first_issue: The central assertion that \(P=\bigcup_n\mathcal P(a_n)\) is finite is false. For example, starting with \(a_1=6\) produces \(6,8,10,12,\ldots\), whose terms collectively have infinitely many prime divisors.
grade.summary: The submission correctly obtains bounded gaps and introduces the globally admissible set \(C\), but its decisive finiteness argument concerns a set of primes that need not be finite. The claim that infinitely many primes force a new prime exceeding \(a_n+M\) is invalid, as is the subsequent asymptotic inequality. Consequently, periodicity of \(C\) is not established. The final passage from eventual behavior to periodicity for every index is also unsupported.
strengths: Correctly proves that every term belongs to \(C\) and that the gaps satisfy \(a_{n+1}-a_n\le M\).
Correctly observes that a finite prime universe would make the admissibility conditions periodic.

errors.description: The claimed finiteness of all prime divisors appearing among the sequence terms is false and is essential to the proof.
Infinitude of \(P\) does not imply that some newly appearing prime satisfies \(p>a_n+M\); new primes can appear gradually below the current term.
The assertion \((a_n+M)/p<2\) “for \(a_n\) large enough” is backwards for fixed \(p\).
Eventual stabilization of \(C_n\) would not by itself justify periodicity at all earlier indices; the required exact-enumeration argument is not given.
